podcast.title: Post-Label Goth Period (1984-1985)
podcast.body: After being dropped by his record label, Jourgensen spent 1984 and 1985 dabbling in goth music, before forging a new direction for his career. "But in 1984, 1985, Alan dabbled in golf music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaboration with Adrian Sherwood (1986)
podcast.body: In 1986, through connections related to Depeche Mode, Jourgensen partnered with producer Adrian Sherwood, whose radical remixing style, emphasizing heavy percussion, electronic rhythm, distortion, and tape loops, greatly influenced Jourgensen and led to the album "Twitch." "But in 1986, through some Depeche Mode connections, he hooked up with producer Adrian Sherwood."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Meek Technopop Ways" Epiphany
podcast.body: Al Jourgensen experienced a transformative moment at a Front 242 concert in Chicago, which is said to have revealed the "error of his meek, techno pop ways" and catalyzed his band's shift towards a more aggressive industrial sound. "But legend has it that it was at a Front II-IV II show in Chicago that Alan Durgensen had as epiphany, of sorts, the one that showed him the error of his meek, techno pop ways."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Career as "Alan"
podcast.body: Before Ministry, Al Jourgensen (referred to as "Alan") was in a Technopop band from Chicago that toured with Depeche Mode and Culture Club. He initially tried to play the "corporate game" for his record company before being dropped. "Alan was in a Tectopop band from Chicago that had spent some time touring with both Depeche Mode and Culture Club."

xref.title: Producer for Ministry's "Twitch" (1986)
xref.body: In 1986, Al Jourgensen collaborated with Adrian Sherwood to produce the album "Twitch." Jourgensen was drawn to Sherwood's signature style of heavy percussion, electronic rhythm, distortion, and tape loops. "He jumped at the chance to work with Adrian. And the result was the 1986 album entitled Twitch."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Transition to Industrial Sound (1986)
xref.body: After being dropped by his record label and dabbling in goth music (1984-1985), Al Jourgensen restarted his career. In 1986, through Depeche Mode connections, he collaborated with producer Adrian Sherwood. Sherwood's radical remixes (e.g., for Depeche Mode) impressed Jourgensen with their heavy percussion, electronic rhythm, distortion, and tape loops, leading to the industrial-leaning album "Twitch." "But in 1986, through some Depeche Mode connections, he hooked up with producer Adrian Sherwood."

xref.title: Give It Away Remix (1991) – Ministry's Al Jourgensen Used a Stoned Chicken on the Mixing Console
xref.body: Al Jourgensen was invited by the Red Hot Chili Peppers to produce a remix of "Give It Away" for their *Blood Sugar Sex Magik* album. His reported method: he brought a live chicken into the studio, blew marijuana smoke in its face until the bird was intoxicated, then let the stoned chicken stagger across the mixing desk. Wherever the chicken left a dropping, Jourgensen made an adjustment to the mix. "He brought a chicken into the studio and blew pot smoke in the chicken's face... Where the chicken pooped, Al made an adjustment to the mix."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Eddie Vedder, Chris Cornell, and Al Jourgensen – Bile Beer Drinking Contest at Lollapalooza 1992
xref.body: The 1992 Lollapalooza tour featured the Jim Rose Circus sideshow, including performer Matt "the Tube" Crowley, who would pump beer, ketchup, chocolate, and Pepto-Bismol into his stomach via a seven-foot swallowed tube and then pump it back out as "bile beer" for audience members to drink. Eddie Vedder, Chris Cornell (Soundgarden), and Al Jourgensen (Ministry) entered a competition for who could drink the most bile beer. Cornell tried and retched; Jourgensen managed it two days in a row; Eddie was there every single night and claimed to have drunk two quarts more than anyone. When asked why, Eddie said: "Just looking for attention." "Eddie won this contest. He called it Wayne."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Lollapalooza "Party in a Bottle" Incident (1992)
xref.body: Backstage at Lollapalooza in 1992, Al Jourgensen forced someone to drink from a bottle of Bushmills whiskey with a broken, jagged neck, threatening physical harm if they refused. It was later revealed that Jourgensen was known to add a "dollop of acid" to his Bushmills, creating what he referred to as a "party in a bottle," though this particular addition fortunately did not occur that day. "I ended up backstage with Al at Lala Paloza in 1992 and he made me drink from a bottle of bush mill whiskey that had dropped on the pavement."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: 2010 Ulcer Rupture and Cardiac Arrest
xref.body: In 2010, after experiencing prolonged vomiting of blood, Al Jourgensen collapsed and was hospitalized, where he went into cardiac arrest multiple times. Doctors discovered he had a ruptured ulcer, one of 13 scattered throughout his stomach and intestines, with one ulcer positioned over an artery. When that ulcer ruptured, it caused the artery to rupture as well, nearly killing him. "In 2010, he finally collapsed and was rushed to hospital where he went into cardiac arrest several times. Eventually, it was determined that Al was suffering from a ruptured ulcer, and when they opened him up, they found 13 ulcers scattered throughout his stomach and intestines. One of them was perched over an artery. Once that ulcer ruptured, so did the artery, and that's what nearly killed him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Addiction Philosophy and Social Circle
xref.body: John Frusciante's perspective on his addiction was intrinsically linked to his depression, leading him to believe he should be perpetually on drugs because they brought him happiness. He explicitly stated, "I was very sad and I was always happy when I was on drugs. Therefore I should be on drugs all the time. I was never guilty. I was always proud to be an addict." During this period, his social circle included many drug-using companions, notably the actor River Phoenix, who would soon die, and Al Jourgensen. "I was very sad and I was always happy when I was on drugs. Therefore I should be on drugs all the time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Al Jourgensen's "Give It Away" Remix Involvement
xref.body: John Frusciante was in the studio with Al Jourgensen when Jourgensen was tasked with creating a new mix of the Red Hot Chili Peppers' hit song "Give It Away." This session became legendary for Jourgensen's bizarre method of remixing, which involved bringing a chicken into the studio, making it stoned with pot smoke, and then adjusting the audio mix based on where the chicken defecated on the mixing board. "Two guys that were definitely badly lost for a long, long time."

xref.title: Al Jourgensen's Alias (Hypo Luxa)
xref.body: Al Jourgensen used the alias Hypo Luxa when producing Nine Inch Nails' cover of "Get Down Make Love." "If you look at the credits, you'll see that it was produced by someone named Hypo Luxa, which is actually El Jorgonson of Ministry."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Al Jourgensen's Backstage Antics at Lollapalooza '92
xref.body: At the Canadian stop of the 1992 Lollapalooza Festival in Barrie, north of Toronto, Ministry's leader Al Jourgensen engaged in notorious backstage behavior. This included throwing various pieces of furniture out of his trailer, drinking from a broken bottle of Bushmills whiskey, and then coercing an observer to help him arrange the discarded furniture into a makeshift "living room" on the concrete. "The last thing to come out of the trailer was Al Jorgensen, the leader of ministry and he was carrying this broken bottle of Bush Mills whiskey."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Al Jourgensen's Early Addiction and Leary Association
xref.body: Al Jourgensen's substance abuse began remarkably early, starting smoking at age 10 and consuming a pack a day by 15. He later became a heavy user of cocaine and heroin. Notably, he lived with LSD advocate Timothy Leary for two years, during which Jourgensen claims he served as Leary's "human guinea pig," a role he cannot fully define. "He started smoking at 10 and was doing a pack of day by the time he was 15."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Associated with Wax Trax
xref.body: Ministry, fronted by Al Jourgensen, was one of the bands associated with Wax Trax of Chicago, a specialist indie label for heavy music that appeared around 1990. "This was the home of Ministry Front II IV II, Front Line Assembly and Dozens More."

xref.title: Association with Al Jourgensen
xref.body: The band Skate Nigs was closely associated with Al Jourgensen of Ministry, and their members frequently contributed to Jourgensen's other musical endeavors. "They were associated with Alan Jorgensen in ministry, and often turned up on some of L's other projects."

xref.title: Assorted Controversial Actions
xref.body: Al Jourgensen has a long history of controversial and confrontational behaviors, including stealing drugs from Courtney Love, physically assaulting R. Kelly for an action that distressed Jourgensen's daughter, and attacking Metallica with vegetables. He also insisted that Limp Bizkit frontman Fred Durst wear nothing but a cowboy hat during a vocal session he produced, blew up Ministry's tour bus with a large firework purchased from a homeless person, and was ejected from the Grammy Awards for screaming at Beyoncé. "Al Jorgensen stole drugs from Courtney Love. He punched out our kelly for doing something that freaked out his daughter. He attacked Metallica with some vegetables."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bar Fight While Sober
xref.body: Despite being clean, sober, and having lost most of his liver, Al Jourgensen still attracts trouble. In one incident at a bar, admiring bikers repeatedly bought him shots. His refusal to drink them, due to his sobriety, insulted the bikers, which then led to a fight breaking out. "He was in a bar once where a bunch of admiring bikers kept buying him shots. But because Al was straight and sober, not to mention without most of his liver, he didn't drink him."

xref.body: Al Jourgensen was commissioned to create a new mix of the Red Hot Chili Peppers' hit song "Give It Away" from their album "Blood Sugar Sex Magik," working with John Frusciante in the studio. "The story is that Al brought a chicken with him and let the chicken wander all over the mixing board."

xref.title: Kubrick's "AI" Film Project and Jourgensen's Antics
xref.body: Al Jourgensen was reportedly approached by director Stanley Kubrick to compose music for a new film titled "AI." Despite Kubrick's admiration for Ministry, Jourgensen repeatedly insisted that "AI" actually stood for "anal intruder" and suggested the project should instead be a porn film. Following Kubrick's death, Steven Spielberg had to intervene to "clean things up" and resolve the situation caused by Jourgensen's disruptive behavior regarding the film. "He somehow got mixed up with director Stanley Kubrick, who wanted him to write music for a new film. He was going to call AI."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Life-Threatening Health Crises
xref.body: Al Jourgensen experienced a near-fatal overdose on New Year's Eve 1992, during which he was clinically dead for a period. He contracted Hepatitis C from a contaminated needle and suffered a toe infection from excessive injecting, which led to gangrene and required amputation. He also almost lost an arm after being bitten by a spider. In addition to heroin and cocaine, he extensively used crack, ketamine, and meth. His ultimate decision to stop drug use came after his gastrointestinal tract exploded, resulting in the loss of 65% of his blood and another clinical death experience. "Al ended up with Hepp C from a contaminated needle. After injecting a toe so much, it turned gangrous and he had to have it amputated."

xref.title: Ministry's Outtakes Project
xref.body: 1000 Homo DJs served as a "goofy side project" initiated by Al Jourgensen of Ministry to release material, specifically Ministry outtakes, while maintaining a clear separation from the main band. The project involved all contributing members adopting fake names for their credits, including Jourgensen (Lux/Buck Satan), Paul Barker (Pan/Officer Aggro), and William Rieflin (We Willy Riefer), and famously included uncredited vocals from Trent Reznor. "He started a goofy side project called 1000 Home Old DJs as a way of releasing some ministry outtakes while keeping things separate from his main band."

xref.title: Ministry/Butthole Surfers Collaboration Recording
xref.body: Al Jourgensen recorded a song with Gibby Haynes of the Butthole Surfers, a process complicated by Haynes being extremely high throughout the entire session. Haynes was only capable of screaming through a megaphone and eventually fell off his stool. Jourgensen dedicated two weeks to meticulously editing all of Haynes's vocal tracks to create usable material for the song. "Gibby was so high the entire time that the only thing he could do is scream stuff through a megaphone and then he fell off his stool."

xref.body: The other notable member, Nivek Ogre, has participated in various other bands, including Ministry with Al Jourgensen, and has developed an interest in working on low-budget horror films, with "Queen of Blood" being a mentioned example. "The other member of note is Nivik Ogre. He's been in a bunch of other bands, including Ministry with Al Jorgensen, but he really seems to enjoy working in low budget horror films. You might want to look up a movie called Queen of Blood."

xref.title: Radical Remixes for Depeche Mode
xref.body: Adrian Sherwood created "pretty radical remixes" for Depeche Mode songs like "People Are People" and "Master and Servant," characterized by heavy percussion, electronic rhythm, distortion, and tape loops. These remixes were highly influential, particularly on Al Jourgensen of Ministry. "Adrian had created some pretty radical remixes for Depeche Mode, most notably for people are people and master and servant."

xref.title: Secret Recording as 1000 Homo DJs
xref.body: During his contract dispute with TVT Records, Trent Reznor secretly recorded vocals on a cover of Black Sabbath's "Supernaut" for the Ministry spin-off band 1000 Homo DJs. There is a dispute whether his vocals actually appear on most versions; only versions specifically labeled "Trent Rezner Vocal Version" feature his voice, otherwise it's Al Jourgensen's voice with distortion. "The result was that Trent had to record secretly and under fake names. One such recording was a ministry spin-off band called 1000 homo DJs."
